But my father was there to comfort me, replacing painful memories with bright hopes. Grief itself seemed sweet when it gave him the chance to dry my tears.

At other times he drew my mind away from my sorrow by comparing it with the despair he had felt at my mother’s death. Even then, his account of his emotions made me shudder. He possessed a poet’s imagination, and when he described the whirlwind that had torn through him, his words brought it to life so vividly that I believed every word as I trembled. I wondered how he had ever returned to the ordinary duties of life after thoughts so wild had seemed to connect him with another world. The ideas he expressed were so overwhelming that the human heart seemed too limited to contain them. His feelings belonged more naturally to a spirit inhabiting earthquakes and volcanoes than to someone enclosed in a mortal body and a human shape. Yet these were only memories; he had changed since then. Now he was all love and tenderness. When I looked up at him in wonder as he spoke, the smile on his lips assured me that only the gentlest emotions ruled his heart.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father guided me into more demanding studies than I had pursued before. My progress delighted him. He stayed with me while I studied, helping with or joining in every lesson. We mixed with many people, and he never let a day pass without trying to enrich it with some fresh enjoyment. His tender attachment to me, and the love and reverence with which I answered it, gave every moment its charm. The hours moved slowly because we used every minute. In one week we experienced more than many people do in several months, and the variety and freshness of our pleasures made each one more enjoyable.

We were constantly going on excursions together. Whether we went to admire beautiful scenery, to look at fine paintings, or sometimes simply to find whatever amusement chance might offer, I was always happy at my father’s side. I regretted every occasion when a third person joined us. Yet if I turned towards him with a troubled look, I found his eyes resting on me, shining with tenderness, and joy returned to my heart at once. Oh, those hours of intense happiness! Brief though they were, they seem as long as an entire lifetime when I look back through the mist of grief that rose immediately afterwards, as though to hide them from me.

“You have not lived in Bath long enough,” he said, “to acquire a taste for its evening parties.”

“Oh, no. Their ordinary nature offers me nothing. I do not play cards.”

“You did not formerly, I know. Cards never used to please you; but time alters a great deal.”

“I have not changed so much as that yet,” Anne exclaimed, then checked herself, afraid of some interpretation she could scarcely define. A few moments passed before he spoke again, apparently from the impulse of the moment: “It is a long time, certainly! Eight and a half years is a long time.”

Whether he might have said more was left for Anne’s imagination to consider at some quieter hour. His words were still sounding in her ears when Henrietta abruptly recalled her to other matters. Eager to seize their present opportunity of going out, she urged her companions to hurry, before another visitor arrived.

They had to rise. Anne declared herself entirely ready and endeavoured to appear so. Yet she felt that if Henrietta had understood the regret and unwillingness with which she left her chair and prepared to leave the room, her own feelings for her cousin—even the certainty of his love—would have taught her to pity Anne.

Their preparations, however, came to a sudden halt. Ominous sounds announced more visitors, and the door opened to admit Sir Walter and Miss Elliot. Their arrival appeared to chill everybody. Anne immediately felt constrained, and saw evidence of the same feeling wherever she turned. All the room’s ease, liberty, and merriment disappeared, subdued into cold reserve, resolute silence, or empty conversation by the unfeeling elegance of her father and sister. How humiliating to know it was so!

In one respect her watchful eye was reassured. Both greeted Captain Wentworth again, and Elizabeth did so more kindly than before. She even spoke to him once, and glanced at him more than once. In fact, Elizabeth was contemplating an important step, as the sequel soon revealed. After several minutes had been expended on the customary trifles, she delivered an invitation intended to discharge all her remaining obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends; nothing formal.” She expressed it all with great grace. The cards she had brought, announcing “Miss Elliot at home,” were placed upon the table, accompanied by a courteous smile embracing the whole party, with one card and one smile directed more particularly towards Captain Wentworth. The fact was that Elizabeth had spent enough time in Bath to appreciate the value of a man with his bearing and appearance.

Sydney Carton stopped in the street, still uncertain where to go. “At Tellson’s bank at nine,” he said thoughtfully. “Would it be wise to let myself be seen in the meantime? I think it would. These people had better know that a man like me is here. It’s a sensible precaution, and may be a necessary first step. But carefully, carefully, carefully! I must think it through.”

He checked his steps, which had already begun carrying him towards a destination, and walked back and forth in the darkening street, following the idea through to its possible consequences. This confirmed his first judgment. “It is best,” he said, his decision finally made, “that these people should know a man like me is here.” He turned towards Saint Antoine.

That day Defarge had described himself as the owner of a wine-shop in the suburb of Saint Antoine. Someone who knew the city well could easily find the place without asking directions. Once Carton had located it, he left the narrower streets, ate dinner at an eating-house, and fell into a deep sleep afterwards. For the first time in years, he drank no spirits. Since the previous night, he had had only a little weak, light wine; and that night he had slowly poured his brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth, like a man finished with drinking it.

It was seven o’clock by the time he woke, refreshed, and went back out into the streets. On his way towards Saint Antoine he paused at a shop window containing a mirror. He made slight adjustments to his disordered loose cravat, his coat collar, and his unruly hair. Then he continued straight to Defarge’s and went inside.

The only customer happened to be Jacques Three, the man with the constantly moving fingers and the croaking voice. Carton had seen him serving on the jury. He stood drinking at the small counter and talking with Defarge and his wife. The Vengeance joined in their conversation as though she were a regular member of the household.

Carton entered, sat down, and asked in very poor French for a small measure of wine. Madame Defarge glanced at him casually, then looked more closely, and then more closely still. Finally she approached him herself and asked what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, raising her dark eyebrows with interest.

He stared at her as though even the sound of a single French word took time to convey its meaning to him. Then he answered in the same strong foreign accent as before.
